A user congratulated the WorkOS team and said its 'extremely pleasant wrapper over SSO and SCIM' made their side project possible instead of 'a nightmare of integrations'.

A customer says WorkOS saved them 'tons of time in both engineering and support cases.' Their own customers often compliment them on how easy SAML and SCIM configuration is, 'but it's really WorkOS's wizard that they are complimenting.'
Another user said they love the simplicity and appreciate that WorkOS takes away 'the headache that is SSO.'
A commenter was confused by the marketing: WorkOS talks about adding all kinds of enterprise features, but they mainly saw SSO in the examples and copy, and asked whether there was anything else.

One commenter estimated that implementing SSO with WorkOS's flexibility and ease of use would take months, mainly because of its built-in integrations with many providers. They added that 'the price is pretty steep,' so it would mostly suit big-budget enterprise software companies.
Comparing pricing, a user said they like Auth0 because it's free for up to 7K active users, while 'WorkOS seems much more expensive out of the gate ($49 per "connection"?).'

A commenter pushed back on the claim that SSO takes months to build: implementing the OIDC flow from scratch 'takes half a day to get working and maybe a week to polish,' and libraries make it faster.

Another commenter argued that an SSO login wall is the most trivial enterprise feature, with plenty of libraries available, so WorkOS 'won't be a game changer, at least not with its current feature set.' They said compliance, data residency, eDiscovery, RBAC, SLAs and MDM would interest customers far more.

A user raised lock-in concerns: you pay someone else to hold critical customer login data. They asked how you would get it out, what that costs, and whether there are contractual guarantees. They also noted that customer-side IdP setup makes moving away from WorkOS hard to manage.

Speaking from experience, a commenter said products that gain traction often hit a brick wall entering the enterprise market. Teams stop core feature work to add hacky enterprise features and take on tech debt, so a developer-friendly drop-in SaaS like WorkOS 'could be a huge win.'

An IdP-side admin applauded the idea (though they dislike the name). They said a staggering number of externally developed apps fail to authenticate to their IdP even after dozens of calls walking developer teams through the OIDC flow.

A SAML service provider asked WorkOS to supply editable IdP setup docs (Okta, Azure ADFS, etc.) to hand to their own customers. They said the biggest SAML pain is customers who only understand their IdP, and that the support burden of SAML is a big reason the 'sso.tax' exists.
One commenter wrote: 'Very impressed with how the documentation looks. Similar to ReadMe.io, but a little bit more simple.'

Someone in a regulated industry (life sciences/pharma) said SSO/SAML, SCIM and audit logs are all challenges they had to tackle as one-offs for their SaaS, so they appreciated WorkOS's bundled approach.

Another commenter raised an adoption barrier: enterprise subcontractors must be listed in contracts and approved by clients. They would pay for WorkOS but want to run it under something like AWS Marketplace to avoid collecting client signatures over who accesses personal data and where it's hosted.

On audit logs, a user said they couldn't see how WorkOS differs from analytics tools like Amplitude or Mixpanel, since you declare events the same way. They also said the docs don't explain how the audit trail is made available to end customers.
Other early comments: 'I wish I would have found this 3 month ago,' and a note that RBAC wasn't available yet, with a request for a timeline.

A user who moved from a startup to a large company called WorkOS 'extremely impressive,' saying the value prop resonates. They described the third-party compliance and enterprise IT requirements small shops face as 'mind boggling.'
